claim: Ric-8A has guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity for several classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits in vertebrates.
source: Cytosolic Ric-8A has guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity and is a chaperone for several classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of Ric-8A, supported by the citation (Tall et al., 2003) in the introduction.

claim: Ric-8A is a chaperone for several classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits in vertebrates.
source: Cytosolic Ric-8A has guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity and is a chaperone for several classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Chan et al., 2013).

claim: Ric-8A disrupts the secondary structure of the Gα Ras-like domain that girds the guanine nucleotide-binding site.
source: Using Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange-Mass Spectrometry (HDX-MS) we show that Ric-8A disrupts the secondary structure of the Gα Ras-like domain that girds the guanine nucleotide-binding site, and destabilizes the interface between the Gαi1 Ras and helical domains, allowing domain separation and nucleotide release.
evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: Ric-8A destabilizes the interface between the Gαi1 Ras and helical domains, allowing domain separation and nucleotide release.
source: Using Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange-Mass Spectrometry (HDX-MS) we show that Ric-8A disrupts the secondary structure of the Gα Ras-like domain that girds the guanine nucleotide-binding site, and destabilizes the interface between the Gαi1 Ras and helical domains, allowing domain separation and nucleotide release.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data in the manuscript (Figures 4, 6) and previous DEER experiments (Van Eps et al., 2015).

claim: Changes induced by Ric-8A are largely reversed upon binding GTP and dissociation of Ric-8A.
source: These changes are largely reversed upon binding GTP and dissociation of Ric-8A.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data comparing Gαi1•GDP, Gαi1:Ric-8A, and Gαi1•GTPγS states (Figures 2, 4).

claim: HDX-MS identifies a potential Gα interaction site in Ric-8A.
source: HDX-MS identifies a potential Gα interaction site in Ric-8A.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing protection of residues 454-470 in Ric-8A upon Gαi1 binding (Figure 3, Figure 7a).

claim: Alanine scanning reveals residues crucial for GEF activity within the sequence 454-470 of Ric-8A.
source: Alanine scanning reveals residues crucial for GEF activity within that sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from alanine mutagenesis and GEF activity assays (Figure 7b, Table 1).

claim: Ric-8A binds the C-terminus of Gα, similar to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: HDX confirms that, like G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), Ric-8A binds the C-terminus of Gα.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing protection of the C-terminus of Gαi1 (Figure 4a) and previous studies (Papasergi et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2011).

claim: In contrast to GPCRs, Ric-8A interacts with Switches I and II of Gα.
source: In contrast to GPCRs, Ric-8A interacts with Switches I and II of Gα and possibly at the Gα domain interface.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing protection of Switch I and Switch II regions (Figure 4a, Figure 5a) and EPR studies (Van Eps et al., 2015).

claim: Ric-8A possibly interacts at the Gα domain interface.
source: In contrast to GPCRs, Ric-8A interacts with Switches I and II of Gα and possibly at the Gα domain interface.
evidence: This is inferred from HDX-MS data showing changes at the domain interface (Figure 6) and DEER spectroscopy results (Van Eps et al., 2015).

claim: Ric-8A catalyzes the release of GDP from i, q and 13-classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits (Gα) in vitro.
source: Resistance to Inhibitors of Cholinesterase 8A (Ric-8A) is a 59.7 KDa protein that catalyzes the release of GDP from i, q and 13-classes of heterotrimeric G protein α subunits (Gα) in vitro (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Tall et al., 2003.

claim: Ric-8A is the best characterized of the family of cytosolic proteins with guanine nucleotide exchange (GEF) activity at Gα subunits.
source: In that capacity, Ric-8A is the best characterized of the family of cytosolic proteins with guanine nucleotide exchange (GEF) activity at Gα subunits.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors act upon heterotrimeric complexes of Gα and G protein beta-gamma heterodimers (Gβγ).
source: Unlike G protein-coupled receptors, which act upon heterotrimeric complexes of Gα and G protein beta-gamma heterodimers (Gβγ), Ric-8A acts exclusively at GDP-bound Gα.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR function.

claim: Ric-8A acts exclusively at GDP-bound Gα.
source: Unlike G protein-coupled receptors, which act upon heterotrimeric complexes of Gα and G protein beta-gamma heterodimers (Gβγ), Ric-8A acts exclusively at GDP-bound Gα.
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Tall et al., 2003) and is a key distinguishing feature of Ric-8A.

claim: Ric-8A GEF activity is unidirectional.
source: GEF activity is unidirectional; Ric-8A does not interact with Gα•GTP, nor does the Gα•Ric-8A complex dissociate in the presence of GDP (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tall et al., 2003.

claim: Ric-8A does not interact with Gα•GTP.
source: GEF activity is unidirectional; Ric-8A does not interact with Gα•GTP, nor does the Gα•Ric-8A complex dissociate in the presence of GDP (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tall et al., 2003.

claim: The Gα•Ric-8A complex does not dissociate in the presence of GDP.
source: GEF activity is unidirectional; Ric-8A does not interact with Gα•GTP, nor does the Gα•Ric-8A complex dissociate in the presence of GDP (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tall et al., 2003.

claim: Ric-8A is structurally unrelated to GPCRs.
source: Ric-8A is structurally unrelated to GPCRs.
evidence: This is a statement of structural comparison based on known protein structures.

claim: The circular dichroic spectrum of mammalian Ric-8A indicates that it is a predominantly alpha-helical protein.
source: The circular dichroic spectrum of mammalian Ric-8A indicates that it is a predominantly alpha-helical protein (Figueroa et al., 2009; Thomas et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Figueroa et al., 2009 and Thomas et al., 2011.

claim: Amino acid sequence analysis suggests that Ric-8A adopts an armadillo-repeat fold similar to that of β-catenin and its structural analogs.
source: amino acid sequence analysis suggests that Ric-8A adopts an armadillo-repeat fold similar to that of β-catenin and its structural analogs (Figueroa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Figueroa et al., 2009 and sequence analysis methods.

claim: Nuclear import proteins are regulated by the Ras family G protein Ran.
source: Among the latter are nuclear import proteins that are regulated by the Ras family G protein Ran (Vetter et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vetter et al., 1999.

claim: smgGDS is a GEF for certain Rho-family G proteins.
source: and smgGDS, a GEF for certain Rho-family G proteins (Hamel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hamel et al., 2011.

claim: In C. elegans, Drosophila and mouse, Ric-8A orthologs have been identified as regulators of synaptic transmission.
source: In C. elegans, Drosophila and mouse, Ric-8A orthologs (generally, Ric-8) have been identified as regulators of synaptic transmission and of mitotic spindle movement in asymmetric cell division (Afshar et al., 2004; Couwenbergs et al., 2004; David et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005; Miller and Rand, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different organisms.

claim: In C. elegans, Drosophila and mouse, Ric-8A orthologs have been identified as regulators of mitotic spindle movement in asymmetric cell division.
source: In C. elegans, Drosophila and mouse, Ric-8A orthologs (generally, Ric-8) have been identified as regulators of synaptic transmission and of mitotic spindle movement in asymmetric cell division (Afshar et al., 2004; Couwenbergs et al., 2004; David et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005; Miller and Rand, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different organisms.

claim: Ric-8 orthologs may function as components of G Protein Regulator (GPR/Goloco)-signaling complexes with Gα in mitotic spindle movement.
source: In the latter role, Ric-8 orthologs may function as components of G Protein Regulator (GPR/Goloco)-signaling complexes with Gα (Woodard et al., 2010; Oner et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Ric-8 has roles in amplification of G protein signaling in chemotaxis by Dictyostelium.
source: Roles in amplification of G protein signaling in chemotaxis by Dictyostelium (Kataria et al., 2013) and synaptic transmission in C. elegans (Miller et al., 2000; Reynolds et al., 2005) have also been described.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kataria et al., 2013.

claim: Ric-8 has roles in synaptic transmission in C. elegans.
source: Roles in amplification of G protein signaling in chemotaxis by Dictyostelium (Kataria et al., 2013) and synaptic transmission in C. elegans (Miller et al., 2000; Reynolds et al., 2005) have also been described.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2000 and Reynolds et al., 2005.

claim: There is no direct evidence that Ric-8A is a physiological GEF.
source: There is no direct evidence that Ric-8A is a physiological GEF.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of evidence in the field.

claim: The observation of Ric-8A-enhanced Gβγ-dependent signaling after peptide-induced disruption of G protein heterotrimers is consistent with in vivo GEF activity.
source: However the observation of Ric-8A-enhanced Gβγ-dependent signaling after peptide-induced disruption of G protein heterotrimers is consistent with in vivo GEF activity (Malik et al., 2005)
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations cited from Malik et al., 2005.

claim: Ric-8A is present in mitotic spindle-associated complexes.
source: as is its presence in the mitotic spindle-associated complexes described above.
evidence: This is inferred from the earlier discussion of Ric-8 in mitotic spindle movement.

claim: Ric-8 facilitates the biogenesis of active Gα proteins in eukaryotic cells.
source: Recent studies have provided evidence that Ric-8 facilitates the biogenesis of active Gα proteins in eukaryotic cells and their localization to intracellular membranes and the cell cortex (Gabay et al., 2011; Hampoelz et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ric-8 facilitates the localization of Gα proteins to intracellular membranes and the cell cortex.
source: Recent studies have provided evidence that Ric-8 facilitates the biogenesis of active Gα proteins in eukaryotic cells and their localization to intracellular membranes and the cell cortex (Gabay et al., 2011; Hampoelz et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ric-8 orthologs function as molecular chaperones for Gα.
source: Ric-8 orthologs function as molecular chaperones for Gα (Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2013.

claim: Ric-8 blocks the degradation of Gα subunits by inhibiting their ubiquitination.
source: By inhibiting their ubiquitination, Ric-8 also blocks the degradation of Gα subunits (Nagai et al., 2010; Chishiki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nagai et al., 2010 and Chishiki et al., 2013.

claim: Whether Ric-8 isoforms have dual physiological functions as both chaperones and GEFs has not been resolved.
source: Whether Ric-8 isoforms have dual physiological functions as both chaperones and GEFs has not been resolved (Blumer and Lanier, 2014; Tall, 2013; Hinrichs et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about an unresolved question in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Ric-8A is essential for mammalian development.
source: In any case, Ric-8A is essential for mammalian development.
evidence: This is supported by the following statement about Ric-8A knockout mice.

claim: Ric-8A (-/-) mutant mouse embryos cannot progress beyond the initial stages of gastrulation and die during early embryogenesis.
source: Ric-8A (-/-) mutant mouse embryos cannot progress beyond the initial stages of gastrulation and die during early embryogenesis (Tõnissoo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tõnissoo et al., 2010.

claim: Gα subunits are members of the Ras superfamily of regulatory GTP binding proteins.
source: Gα subunits are members of the Ras superfamily of regulatory GTP binding proteins (Gilman, 1987; Sprang, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gα bear polypeptide segments called Switch I and Switch II that flank the GTP binding site.
source: Characteristic of the superfamily, Gα bear polypeptide segments called Switch I and Switch II that flank the GTP binding site.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Gα proteins.

claim: Switch I and Switch II undergo conformational transitions upon GTP hydrolysis that are typically coupled to the loss of affinity for effectors and an increase in affinity for Gβγ.
source: These segments are observed to undergo conformational transitions upon GTP hydrolysis that are typically coupled to the loss of affinity for effectors and an increase in affinity for Gβγ (Lambright et al., 1994; Mixon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Gα proteins have a P-loop that encompasses the α and β phosphates of the guanine nucleotide.
source: Other characteristic structural features are a P-loop that encompasses the α and β phosphates of the guanine nucleotide and two loop segments that form conserved contacts with the purine ring (Noel et al., 1993; Coleman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gα proteins have two loop segments that form conserved contacts with the purine ring.
source: Other characteristic structural features are a P-loop that encompasses the α and β phosphates of the guanine nucleotide and two loop segments that form conserved contacts with the purine ring (Noel et al., 1993; Coleman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gα subunits have an insertion of a ~110 residue alpha helical domain at the N-terminus of Switch I.
source: Gα subunits are also distinctive among Ras superfamily members in the insertion of a ~110 residue alpha helical domain at the N-terminus of Switch I.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Gα proteins.

claim: The helical domain blocks egress of nucleotide from the Ras domain in Gα subunits.
source: The helical domain blocks egress of nucleotide from the Ras domain.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Gα proteins.

claim: GPCRs grasp the C-terminus of Gα and the N-terminus of its β1 strand.
source: G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCR), as exemplified by the complex of the β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR) with the Gs heterotrimer, grasp the C-terminus of Gα and the N-terminus of its β1 strand.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of GPCR-G protein complexes.

claim: GPCR interactions with Gα cause structural perturbations that disrupt the P-loop and purine binding site, and release contacts between the Ras and alpha helical domains, thereby liberating GDP and providing an entry path for GTP.
source: These interactions are proposed to cause structural perturbations that disrupt the P-loop and purine binding site, and release contacts between the Ras and alpha helical domains, thereby liberating GDP and providing an entry path for GTP (Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on structural studies, supported by citation to Rasmussen et al., 2011.

claim: Ric-8A forms a Michaelis complex with Gα•GDP which, in the absence of GTP, releases GDP and forms a stable Gα:Ric-8A intermediate.
source: Ric-8A forms a Michaelis complex with Gα•GDP which, in the absence of GTP, releases GDP and forms a stable Gα:Ric-8A intermediate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tall et al., 2003 and Thomas et al., 2008.

claim: In the presence of GTP, the Gα:Ric-8A complex undergoes an exchange reaction, generating free Ric-8A and Gα•GTP.
source: In the presence of GTP, this complex undergoes an exchange reaction, generating free Ric-8A and Gα•GTP (Tall et al., 2003; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tall et al., 2003 and Thomas et al., 2008.

claim: Gαi1 is conformationally heterogeneous in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
source: Using several biophysical approaches, we demonstrated that Gαi1 is conformationally heterogeneous in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex (Thomas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2011 and multiple biophysical techniques.

claim: Severe attenuation of amide 15N-1H peaks was observed in the TROSY-HSQC spectrum of Gαi1 in complex with Ric-8A.
source: We observed severe attenuation of amide 15N-1H peaks in the TROSY-HSQC spectrum of Gαi1
evidence: This is an experimental observation from NMR spectroscopy.

claim: A doubling in the number of protons that become accessible to proton-deuterium exchange was observed in Gαi1:Ric-8A relative to Gαi1•GDP.
source: and a doubling in the number of protons that become accessible to proton-deuterium exchange relative to Gαi1•GDP.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from HDX studies.

claim: DEER experiments with nitroxide spin-labeled Gαi1 showed extensive broadening in the spectrum of inter-probe distances that accompany displacement of the alpha helical and Ras-like domains of the G protein.
source: Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) experiments with nitroxide spin-labeled Gαi1 showed extensive broadening in the spectrum of inter-probe distances that accompany displacement of the alpha helical and Ras-like domains of the G protein (Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Van Eps et al., 2015.

claim: Ric-8A induces or accommodates large changes in the global structure and dynamic behavior of Gαi1 by stabilizing the nucleotide-free state.
source: In stabilizing the nucleotide-free state, Ric-8A induces or accommodates large changes in the global structure and dynamic behavior of Gαi1.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple biophysical studies cited above.

claim: At near neutral pH, in the seconds-to-hours time regime, continuous exchange experiments report HDX from peptide amide groups.
source: At near neutral pH, in the seconds-to-hours time regime, continuous exchange experiments report HDX from peptide amide groups.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDX-MS methodology.

claim: HDX is suppressed by involvement of backbone amide hydrogen atoms in hydrogen bonds.
source: HDX is suppressed by involvement of backbone amide hydrogen atoms in hydrogen bonds, but enhanced when such interactions are broken and amide groups become accessible to solvent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDX-MS methodology.

claim: HDX is enhanced when hydrogen bond interactions are broken and amide groups become accessible to solvent.
source: HDX is suppressed by involvement of backbone amide hydrogen atoms in hydrogen bonds, but enhanced when such interactions are broken and amide groups become accessible to solvent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDX-MS methodology.

claim: Protein 'breathing' motions that expose amide protons to solvent result in a steady increase in HDX over time.
source: Further, protein 'breathing' motions that expose amide protons to solvent result in a steady increase in HDX over time (Drozdetskiy et al., 2015; Englander and Kallenbach, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDX-MS methodology, supported by citations.

claim: Protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions may induce changes in amide solvent accessibility, protein flexibility and hydrogen bonding, which are manifest in changes in HDX processes.
source: Protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions may induce changes in amide solvent accessibility, protein flexibility and hydrogen bonding, and these are manifest in changes in HDX processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDX-MS methodology.

claim: In the complex with Ric-8A, the peptide amide hydrogen atoms of nucleotide-free Gαi1 become accessible to exchange in amino acids that contact the nucleotide.
source: Here, we show that in the complex with Ric-8A, the peptide amide hydrogen atoms of nucleotide-free Gαi1 become accessible to exchange, not only in amino acids that contact the nucleotide, but also in the scaffold of secondary structure elements that encompass and support the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the complex with Ric-8A, the peptide amide hydrogen atoms of nucleotide-free Gαi1 become accessible to exchange in the scaffold of secondary structure elements that encompass and support the nucleotide-binding site.
source: Here, we show that in the complex with Ric-8A, the peptide amide hydrogen atoms of nucleotide-free Gαi1 become accessible to exchange, not only in amino acids that contact the nucleotide, but also in the scaffold of secondary structure elements that encompass and support the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The direction of HDX changes in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex is essentially the reverse of those observed in the transition from Gαi1•GDP to Gαi1 bound to Mg2+ and GTPγS, although greater in magnitude.
source: The direction of these changes is essentially the reverse of those observed in the transition from Gαi1•GDP to Gαi1 bound to Mg2+ and the slowly hydrolysable GTP analog GTPγS, although greater in magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of HDX-MS data for different states of Gαi1 (Figures 1, 2, 4).

claim: Non-myristoylated rat Gαi1 was used in the HDX experiments.
source: In the experiments described here, we used non-myristoylated rat Gαi1 and rat (1-491) Ric-8A, in which the 29 C-terminal residues of the full-length protein are absent.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials used.

claim: Rat (1-491) Ric-8A, in which the 29 C-terminal residues of the full-length protein are absent, was used in the HDX experiments.
source: In the experiments described here, we used non-myristoylated rat Gαi1 and rat (1-491) Ric-8A, in which the 29 C-terminal residues of the full-length protein are absent.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials used.

claim: C-terminally truncated Ric-8A (1-491) exhibits roughly 10% higher GEF activity than the native protein.
source: This C-terminally truncated Ric-8A exhibits roughly 10% higher GEF activity than the native protein (Thomas et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2008.

claim: The Gαi1:Ric-8A complex remains intact and active in GTPγS uptake throughout the course of the HDX experiment.
source: The Gαi1:Ric-8A complex remains intact and active in GTPγS uptake throughout the course of the of the HDX experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HDX was measured from Gαi1•GDP, Gαi1•GTPγS, Ric-8A and Gαi1:Ric-8A at successive time points ranging from 30 s to 5 hr following dilution of proteins or protein complexes with deuterated buffer.
source: We measured HDX from Gαi1•GDP, Gαi1•GTPγS, Ric-8A and Gαi1:Ric-8A at successive time points ranging from 30 s to 5 hr following dilution of proteins or protein complexes with deuterated buffer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Overlapping peptide fragments recovered from pepsinolysis represent the entire amino acid sequence of Gαi1.
source: In aggregate, overlapping peptide fragments recovered from pepsinolysis represent the entire amino acid sequence of Gαi1 and 87% of that of Ric-8A (Figures 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Overlapping peptide fragments recovered from pepsinolysis represent 87% of the amino acid sequence of Ric-8A.
source: In aggregate, overlapping peptide fragments recovered from pepsinolysis represent the entire amino acid sequence of Gαi1 and 87% of that of Ric-8A (Figures 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The average number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 2.5 for Gαi1.
source: The average and maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 2.5 and 6, respectively, for Gαi1 and 1.7 and 6, respectively for Ric-8A.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the peptide coverage.

claim: The maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 6 for Gαi1.
source: The average and maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 2.5 and 6, respectively, for Gαi1 and 1.7 and 6, respectively for Ric-8A.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the peptide coverage.

claim: The average number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 1.7 for Ric-8A.
source: The average and maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 2.5 and 6, respectively, for Gαi1 and 1.7 and 6, respectively for Ric-8A.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the peptide coverage.

claim: The maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 6 for Ric-8A.
source: The average and maximum number of peptides that overlap with any single residue is 2.5 and 6, respectively, for Gαi1 and 1.7 and 6, respectively for Ric-8A.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the peptide coverage.

claim: The overall pattern of HDX from Gαi1 secondary structures in the GTPγS-bound state is similar to that reported earlier for the GDP•Mg2+AlF complex of Gαi1.
source: The overall pattern of HDX from Gαi1 secondary structures in the GTPγS-bound state is similar to that reported earlier for the GDP•Mg2+AlF complex of Gαi1 published earlier (Preininger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data, supported by citation to Preininger et al., 2012.

claim: Ric-8A binding and GDP release result in structural changes manifested by up to a 40% increase in deuteration (deprotection) of some peptides.
source: Ric-8A binding and GDP release result in structural changes manifested by up to a 40% increase in deuteration (deprotection) of some peptides and a decrease in deuteration exceeding 25% (protection) in others.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Ric-8A binding and GDP release result in structural changes manifested by a decrease in deuteration exceeding 25% (protection) in some peptides.
source: Ric-8A binding and GDP release result in structural changes manifested by up to a 40% increase in deuteration (deprotection) of some peptides and a decrease in deuteration exceeding 25% (protection) in others.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Ric-8A binding does not induce striking changes in slow protein dynamics as measured by the slope of HDX with time.
source: In contrast, Ric-8A binding does not induce striking changes in slow protein dynamics (Figure 1—source data 1) as measured by the slope of HDX with time.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Most of the peptide segments that directly contact the nucleotide-binding scaffold of Gαi1 are deprotected in the Ric-8A-bound state.
source: Most of the peptide segments that directly contact the nucleotide-binding scaffold of Gαi1 are deprotected in the Ric-8A-bound state.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 4a and 5.

claim: The P-loop shows high levels of deprotection in the Ric-8A-bound state.
source: The P-loop, which enfolds the α and β phosphates of bound guanine nucleotides, and the β5-αG loop, which harbors the NPXY motif that determines guanine- specificity at the purine binding sub-site, show high levels of deprotection (Figures 4a and 5, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 4a and 5.

claim: The β5-αG loop shows high levels of deprotection in the Ric-8A-bound state.
source: The P-loop, which enfolds the α and β phosphates of bound guanine nucleotides, and the β5-αG loop, which harbors the NPXY motif that determines guanine- specificity at the purine binding sub-site, show high levels of deprotection (Figures 4a and 5, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 4a and 5.

claim: Backbone amide deprotection extends to the α-helical (αG and a segment of α4) and β-sheet scaffolds (β1, β4 and β5) that support nucleotide-contacting regions.
source: Backbone amide deprotection extends to the α-helical (αG and a segment of α4) and β-sheet scaffolds (β1, β4 and β5) that support these nucleotide-contacting regions (Figure 5b, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Secondary structure elements αG, β4 and β5 support a hydrophobic cluster that supports the purine binding site.
source: Secondary structure elements αG, β4 and β5 in particular support a hydrophobic cluster that supports the purine binding site (Figure 5c, Video 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Increased deuteration of αG, β4 and β5 indicates that the main-chain hydrogen bonding network is destabilized in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
source: Increased deuteration of these segments indicates that this main-chain hydrogen bonding network is destablized in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: Disruption of the hydrogen bonding network could result in disruption of van der Waals interactions within the hydrophobic cluster, resulting in the loss of tertiary structural integrity of the nucleotide-binding site and the surrounding structure.
source: van der Waals interactions within the cluster could in turn be disrupted, resulting in the loss of tertiary structural integrity of the nucleotide-binding site and the surrounding structure.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural principles.

claim: The segment extending from the C-terminus of α4 through β6 is protected by Ric-8A.
source: In contrast, the segment extending from the C-terminus of α4 though β6 is protected by Ric-8A, as is the C-terminus of α5 (see below).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Secondary structure elements at the Ras domain-helical domain interface are destabilized in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
source: Secondary structure elements at the Ras domain-helical domain interface are destabilized in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Conserved residues in αF, α5 and, to a lesser extent, α1 all show increased deuteration in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex.
source: Conserved residues in αF, α5 and, to a lesser extent, α1 all show increased deuteration (Figure 6, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Residues in αF, α5, and α1 contribute to a network of interactions that link the domain interface and the guanine nucleotide-binding site.
source: These residues contribute to a network of interactions that link the domain interface and the guanine nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of Gα proteins.

claim: Destabilization of interactions at the domain interface promotes nucleotide unbinding, domain separation and nucleotide release.
source: It is likely that destabilization of these interactions promotes nucleotide unbinding, domain separation (Van Eps et al., 2015) and nucleotide release.

claim: The αD-αE loop in the helical domain becomes moderately protected in Gαi1:Ric-8A.

claim: The αD-αE loop, together with other features of the helical domain, including αA, may be shielded from solvent by interactions with Ric-8A.
source: The αD-αE loop, together with other features of the helical domain, including αA, may be shielded from solvent by interactions with Ric-8A.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS protection data.

claim: Switch I shows modest protection from HDX in the Ric-8A complex.
source: Switch I (~residues 176–181) and to a greater extent, Switch II (~residues 203–215), show modest protection from HDX in the Ric-8A complex (Figure 4a and Figure 5a, Video 1).

claim: Switch II shows modest protection from HDX in the Ric-8A complex to a greater extent than Switch I.
source: Switch I (~residues 176–181) and to a greater extent, Switch II (~residues 203–215), show modest protection from HDX in the Ric-8A complex (Figure 4a and Figure 5a, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 4a and 5a.

claim: EPR studies show that Gαi1 residues R209 and K180 in Switch I and Switch II, respectively, become partially immobilized upon binding to Ric-8A.
source: Specifically, EPR studies show that Gαi1 residues R209 and K180 in Switch I and Switch II, respectively, become partially immobilized upon binding to Ric-8A (Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Van Eps et al., 2015.

claim: A chimera of Gαs that harbors the Switch II sequence of Gαi1 is not protected from ubiquitination by Ric-8B.
source: The possibility that Switch II is a Ric-8A binding site is also suggested by the observation that a chimera of Gαs that harbors the Switch II sequence of Gαi1 is not protected from ubiquitination by Ric-8B, a Gαs-specific ortholog of Ric-8A (Nagai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nagai et al., 2010.

claim: The C-terminus of Gαi1, including residues of α5, is strongly protected from HDX by Ric-8A.
source: The C-terminus of Gαi1, including residues of α5, is strongly protected from HDX by Ric-8A (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A peptide encompassing the C-terminus sequence of Gαi1 is a competitive inhibitor of Gαi1 for Ric-8A GEF activity.
source: This finding is consistent with other studies that implicate the C-terminus of Gαi1 as a Ric-8A interaction site, including the observation that a peptide encompassing this sequence is a competitive inhibitor of Gαi1 for Ric-8A GEF activity (Papasergi et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Papasergi et al., 2015 and Thomas et al., 2011.

claim: The amino terminus of Gαi1 is protected by Ric-8A.
source: Also protected is the amino terminus of Gαi1, which packs against the C-terminus in crystal structures of Gαi1•GDP that crystallize in space group I4 (Mixon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and structural knowledge from Mixon et al., 1995.

claim: An N-terminal truncation mutant of Gαi1 remains a Ric-8A substrate.
source: Nevertheless, an N-terminal truncation mutant of Gαi1 remains a Ric-8A substrate (Thomas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2011.

claim: A broad interaction surface for Gαi1 with Ric-8A encompasses structural elements of the helical domain near its interface with the Ras domain, extends to Switch I and Switch II, and includes the C-terminus.
source: From the HDX protection data, we infer a broad interaction surface for Gαi1 that encompasses structural elements of the helical domain near its interface with the Ras domain, extends to Switch I and Switch II, and includes the C-terminus, which may make the most intimate contacts with Ric-8A (Figure 4a, Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS protection data.

claim: The C-terminus of Gαi1 may make the most intimate contacts with Ric-8A.
source: From the HDX protection data, we infer a broad interaction surface for Gαi1 that encompasses structural elements of the helical domain near its interface with the Ras domain, extends to Switch I and Switch II, and includes the C-terminus, which may make the most intimate contacts with Ric-8A (Figure 4a, Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS protection data and other studies.

claim: Changes in HD protection that occur upon exchange of GDP for GTPγS are, for the majority of peptides analyzed, less pronounced than those observed when Ric-8A displaces GDP from Gαi1.
source: Changes in HD protection that occur upon exchange of GDP for GTPγS are, for the majority of peptides analyzed, less pronounced than those observed when Ric-8A displaces GDP from Gαi1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the P-loop and α1 at the nucleotide-binding site, changes in the magnitude of HDX upon GTPγS binding are the opposite of those observed in the transition from Gα•GDP to Gα•Ric-8A.
source: In the P-loop and α1 at the nucleotide-binding site, changes in the magnitude of HDX are the opposite of those observed in the transition from Gα•GDP to Gα•Ric-8A.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of HDX-MS data in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: The P-loop and α1 become moderately protected upon GTPγS binding, consistent with structural rigidification induced by nucleotide triphosphate binding.
source: These latter segments become moderately protected, consistent with structural rigidification induced by nucleotide triphosphate binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and structural knowledge.

claim: Modest protection upon GTPγS binding extends to the β4 – Switch III – α3 turn sequence, and αD-αF loop that flanks Switch III in polar inter-domain contacts.
source: Modest protection extends also to the β4 – Switch III – α3 turn sequence, and αD-αF loop that flanks Switch III in polar inter-domain contacts.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Switch III and α3 are consensus effector binding sites of GTP-activated Gα.
source: Notably, Switch III and α3 are consensus effector binding sites of GTP-activated Gα (Sprang et al., 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Sprang et al., 2007.

claim: Protection from HDX of Switch III and α3 could reflect a structural stiffening of these elements in the GTP-bound state.
source: and protection from HDX could reflect a structural stiffening of these elements in the GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and structural knowledge.

claim: The pattern of changes in HDX protection upon transition between GDP and GTPγS-bound states roughly parallel the changes in amide chemical shifts observed in the HSQC spectra of Gαi1.
source: The pattern of changes in HDX protection upon transition between GDP and GTPγS-bound states roughly parallel the changes in amide chemical shifts observed in the HSQC spectra of Gαi1 (Goricanec et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to NMR data, supported by citation to Goricanec et al., 2016.

claim: The C-terminus of β3 and Switch II are protected from HDX by GTPγS binding.
source: The C-terminus of β3 and Switch II are protected from HDX by GTPγS binding.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Residues in the 201-203 segment engage the γ phosphate of GTP.
source: Residues in this segment, particularly the peptide amides of 201–203, engage the γ phosphate of GTP and Asp 200 is hydrogen bonded to a water ligand of the Mg2+ co-factor (Coleman et al., 1994; Coleman and Sprang, 1999).

claim: Asp 200 is hydrogen bonded to a water ligand of the Mg2+ co-factor.
source: Residues in this segment, particularly the peptide amides of 201–203, engage the γ phosphate of GTP and Asp 200 is hydrogen bonded to a water ligand of the Mg2+ co-factor (Coleman et al., 1994; Coleman and Sprang, 1999).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Switch II adopts a more ordered helical conformation and packs against α3 and the β1-β3 scaffold of the Ras domain in the GTP-bound state.
source: Switch II itself, which is poorly ordered in the GDP-bound state, adopts a more ordered helical conformation and packs against α3 and the β1-β3 scaffold of the Ras domain (Mixon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Mixon et al., 1995.

claim: The moderate protection of Switch I in the GTPγS-bound state may reflect the stabilization of this element through interactions of R178 and T181 with the nucleotide triphosphate and the metal cofactor.
source: The moderate protection of Switch I in the GTPγS-bound state may reflect the stabilization of this element though interactions of R178 and T181 with the nucleotide triphosphate and the metal cofactor.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and structural knowledge.

claim: Relative to Gαi1•GDP, switches I and II experience increased protection from HDX in both the Ric-8A and GTPγS complexes, although by different mechanisms.
source: Thus, relative to Gαi1•GDP, switches I and II experience increased protection from HDX in both the Ric-8A and GTPγS complexes, although by different mechanisms: direct interaction with Ric-8A in the first instance, and structural rigidification upon GTPγS•Mg2+ binding in the second.
evidence: This is a synthesis of HDX-MS data and mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The transition from GDP to GTP-bound states does not affect HDX at sequences (β5 - αG and β6 - α5) that contact the guanine base of GTP.
source: The transition from GDP to GTP-bound states does not affect HDX at sequences (β5 - αG and β6 - α5) that contact the guanine base of GTP.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Residues in the β5-αG and β6-α5 segments are well ordered in both GDP and GTP-analog bound complexes of Gαi1 and transducin.
source: This is consistent with crystal structures, which show residues in these two segments to be well ordered in both GTP and GTP-analog bound complexes of Gαi1 and transducin (Mixon et al., 1995; Lambright et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several structural elements show mild deprotection in the GTP-bound state, including αA in the helical domain, and helical segments against which it packs.
source: Several structural elements show mild deprotection in the GTP-bound state. These include αA in the helical domain, and helical segments against which it packs, as well as residues at the N-terminus of β4 and in the α4-β6 purine-binding loop in the Ras domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Residues at the N-terminus of β4 and in the α4-β6 purine-binding loop in the Ras domain show mild deprotection in the GTP-bound state.
source: Several structural elements show mild deprotection in the GTP-bound state. These include αA in the helical domain, and helical segments against which it packs, as well as residues at the N-terminus of β4 and in the α4-β6 purine-binding loop in the Ras domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The three dimensional structure of Ric-8A has not been determined.
source: The three dimensional structure of Ric-8A has not been determined, nor does it have significant amino acid sequence identity to members of any protein families represented in the Protein Data Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of structural knowledge.

claim: Ric-8A does not have significant amino acid sequence identity to members of any protein families represented in the Protein Data Bank.
source: The three dimensional structure of Ric-8A has not been determined, nor does it have significant amino acid sequence identity to members of any protein families represented in the Protein Data Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence analysis results.

claim: Ric-8A is predicted to adopt an armadillo fold, similar to that of β-catenin and nuclear import proteins.
source: In agreement with earlier sequence analysis studies (Figueroa et al., 2009), Ric-8A is predicted to adopt an armadillo fold, similar to that of β-catenin and nuclear import proteins.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and previous sequence analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The Ric-8A models differed mainly with respect to the packing interactions between neighboring helical segments within the ~130 residue C-terminal region and the spatial relationship of the latter to the N-terminal 400 residues.
source: The Ric-8A models differed mainly with respect to the packing interactions between neighboring helical segments within the ~130 residue C-terminal region and the spatial relationship of the latter to the N-terminal 400 residues, suggesting that the two regions constitute distinct structural domains.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The C-terminal ~130 residues and N-terminal 400 residues of Ric-8A constitute distinct structural domains.
source: The Ric-8A models differed mainly with respect to the packing interactions between neighboring helical segments within the ~130 residue C-terminal region and the spatial relationship of the latter to the N-terminal 400 residues, suggesting that the two regions constitute distinct structural domains.
evidence: This is inferred from computational modeling results.

claim: Throughout its primary structure, Ric-8A is highly susceptible to HDX.
source: Throughout its primary structure, Ric-8A is highly susceptible to HDX (Figure 3)
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nearly half of the observed peptide segments of Ric-8A incorporate deuterium at 60% of exchangeable sites.
source: with nearly half of the observed peptide segments incorporating deuterium at 60% of exchangeable sites.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of HDX-MS data.

claim: Upon binding to Gαi1, Ric-8A undergoes changes in accessibility to HDX throughout its amino acid sequence.
source: Upon binding to Gαi1, Ric-8A undergoes changes in accessibility to HDX throughout its amino acid sequence (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Many Ric-8A-derived peptides show 5–15% changes in deuteration relative to free Ric-8A at successive α/α repeats, suggestive of distributive conformational changes.
source: Many Ric-8A-derived peptides show 5–15% changes in deuteration relative to free Ric-8A at successive α/α repeats, suggestive of distributive conformational changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of HDX-MS data.

claim: An extended sequence in Ric-8A from residue 425 to the C-terminus (residue 491) exhibits a 10–15% increase in HDX relative to free Ric-8A.
source: Notably, an extended sequence corresponding to the structural repeats in Ric-8A, from residue 425 to the C-terminus of the construct (residue 491) exhibit an 10–15% increase in HDX relative to free Ric-8A.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: A highly protected peptide comprising residues 454–470 of Ric-8A shows a 25% decrease in deuteration upon Gαi1 binding.
source: This pattern is interrupted by a highly protected (25% decrease in deuteration) peptide comprising residues 454–470, which is rich in proline and acidic residues.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 3 and 7a.

claim: The peptide comprising residues 454–470 of Ric-8A is rich in proline and acidic residues.
source: This pattern is interrupted by a highly protected (25% decrease in deuteration) peptide comprising residues 454–470, which is rich in proline and acidic residues.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Based on sequence analysis of more than 250 Ric-8A homologs, the polypeptide 454-470 is predicted to be largely unstructured.
source: Based on sequence analysis of more than 250 Ric-8A homologs using Jpred4 (Drozdetskiy et al., 2015), this polypeptide is predicted to be largely unstructured.
evidence: This is based on computational sequence analysis using Jpred4.

claim: The substantial protection afforded residues 454–470 in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex implicates this segment to be a possible Gαi1 binding site.
source: The substantial protection afforded residues 454–470 in the Gαi1:Ric-8A complex implicates this segment to be a possible Gαi1 binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS protection data.

claim: Mutation of any of the five hotspot residues (V455, T456, R458, P466 and G469) in Ric-8A resulted in a diminution in the initial rate of GTPγS incorporation to 12–20% that of WT Ric-8A.
source: Mutation of any of the five hotspot residues (V455, T456, R458, P466 and G469) resulted in a diminution in the initial rate of GTPγS incorporation to 12–20% that of WT Ric-8A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from alanine mutagenesis shown in Figure 7b and Table 1.

claim: Most of the Ric-8A mutants were slightly destabilized, with thermal unfolding transitions (Tm) ranging from 38°C to 47°C, relative to WT Ric-8A, which transitions at 47°C.
source: Using differential scanning fluorimetry, we found that most of the mutants were slightly destabilized, with thermal unfolding transitions (Tm) ranging from 38°C to 47°C, relative to WT Ric-8A, which transitions at 47°C (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by differential scanning fluorimetry data shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is no apparent correlation between thermal melting temperature and GEF activity for Ric-8A mutants.
source: There is no apparent correlation between thermal melting temperature and GEF activity for these mutants.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of data in Figures 7b and 8.

claim: C-terminal truncation of Ric-8A at residue 452 results in comparable loss of GEF activity to the hotspot mutants.
source: Comparable loss of GEF activity is achieved by C-terminal truncation of Ric-8A at residue 452, which entirely eliminates the protected sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Table 1.

claim: Alanine mutants at residues 454 and 468 exhibited significantly slower rates for the overall exchange reaction than for exchange from the Gαi1:Ric-8A intermediate.
source: Alanine mutants at residues 454 and 468 exhibited significantly slower rates for the overall exchange reaction than for exchange from the Gαi1:Ric-8A intermediate (p<0.001, P454A and p<0.02, R458A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Table 1.

claim: Mutation of residues 454 and 468 appears to facilitate binding of GTPγS to, or release of Ric-8A from, the Gαi1:Ric-8A intermediate.
source: Mutation of these residues appears to facilitate binding of GTPγS to, or release of Ric-8A from, the Gαi1:Ric-8A intermediate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data for these mutants.

claim: Residues at the N- and C-termini of the protected sequence in Ric-8A interact directly or through an allosteric interaction with the empty nucleotide-binding site of Gαi1 to increase its affinity for GTP.
source: We propose that residues at the N- and C-termini of the protected sequence in Ric-8A interact directly or through an allosteric interaction with the empty nucleotide-binding site of Gαi1 to increase its affinity for GTP.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on HDX-MS and mutagenesis data.

claim: GPCRs and Ric-8A adopt different strategies to induce roughly similar structural transitions in Gα that facilitate nucleotide exchange.
source: The HDX results presented here suggest that GPCRs and Ric-8A adopt different strategies to induce roughly similar structural transitions in Gα that facilitate nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the HDX-MS results and comparison to known GPCR mechanisms.

claim: GPCRs act on Gα•GDP bound to Gβγ, while Ric-8A acts on free Gα•GDP.
source: This is not unexpected, since the two GEFs are structurally unrelated and act on different states of Gα: GPCRs on Gα•GDP bound to Gβγ, and Ric-8A on free Gα•GDP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the different substrates of these GEFs.

claim: A common mechanism of GPCR-mediated activation is largely consequent on binding the C-terminus and displacement of the α5 helix of Gα.
source: Biochemical (Oldham and Hamm, 2008), structural (Van Eps et al., 2015; Westfield et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2011), computational (Dror et al., 2015) and conservation-based modeling studies (Flock et al., 2015) point to a common mechanism of GPCR-mediated activation that is largely consequent on binding the C-terminus and displacement of the α5 helix of Gα.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical, structural, and computational studies.

claim: In the β2AR:Gs complex, the C-terminus of Gα is accommodated by an extensive interface within a cavity formed by the trans-membrane helices of the receptor.
source: In its interaction with GPCRs, as exemplified by the β2AR:Gs complex and the rhodopsin:transducin C-terminal peptide complex (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Scheerer et al., 2008), the C-terminus of Gα is accommodated by an extensive interface within a cavity formed by the trans-membrane helices of the receptor.
evidence: This is based on structural studies, supported by citations.

claim: A more limited contact surface is formed by interaction of the second cytoplasmic loop of β2R with the junction between the N-terminal helix and β1 of Gαs.
source: A more limited contact surface is formed by interaction of the second cytoplasmic loop of β2R with the junction between the N-terminal helix and β1 of Gαs.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of the β2AR:Gs complex.

claim: GPCR interactions induce structural changes in the β6-α5 loop that forms part of the purine binding site, and the P-loop that enfolds the nucleotide phosphates, thus weakening interactions between GDP and the Ras domain of Gα.
source: Together these interactions induce structural changes in the β6-α5 loop that forms part of the purine binding site, and the P-loop that enfolds the nucleotide phosphates, thus weakening interactions between GDP and the Ras domain of Ga (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Dror et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural and computational studies, supported by citations.

claim: In Gi:rhodopsin, the interface between the helical and Ras domains is destabilized, allowing the domains to separate, providing an exit path for the nucleotide.
source: As observed also by DEER spectroscopy in Gi:rhodopsin (Van Eps et al., 2011), the interface between the helical and Ras domains is destabilized, allowing the domains to separate, providing an exit path for the nucleotide.
evidence: This is supported by DEER spectroscopy studies, cited as Van Eps et al., 2011.

claim: HDX studies of β2AR:Gs showed strong protection of the C-terminus of Gαs.
source: Accordingly, HDX studies of β2AR:Gs showed strong protection of the C-terminus of Gαs (Chung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2011.

claim: Interaction with the β2AR induces strong deprotection of the P-loop and the preceding β1 strand as well as the purine binding β6-α5 and β5-αG loops.
source: Interaction with the receptor induces strong deprotection of the P-loop and the preceding the β1 strand as well as the purine binding β6-α5 and β5-αG loops.
evidence: This is based on HDX studies of β2AR:Gs cited as Chung et al., 2011.

claim: Secondary structure elements at the interface of the Ras and helical domains, including α1 and αF, are accessible to HDX in the β2AR:Gs complex.
source: Secondary structure elements at the interface of the Ras and helical domains, including α1 and αF, are accessible to HDX.
evidence: This is based on HDX studies of β2AR:Gs cited as Chung et al., 2011.

claim: The crystal structure of β2AR:Gs shows that Switch II retains its interactions with Gβγ.
source: The crystal structure of β2AR:Gs shows that Switch II retains its interactions with Gβγ as does the N-terminus of Gα.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of β2AR:Gs.

claim: The N-terminus of Gα retains its interactions with Gβγ in the β2AR:Gs complex.
source: The crystal structure of β2AR:Gs shows that Switch II retains its interactions with Gβγ as does the N-terminus of Gα.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of β2AR:Gs.

claim: The heterotrimer remains intact in the β2AR:Gs complex.
source: Consequently, the heterotrimer remains intact.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that Gα remains bound to Gβγ.

claim: In the β2AR:Gs complex, Gαs appears to be relatively well-ordered.
source: While, in the latter complex, Gαs appears to be relatively well-ordered
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis.

claim: NMR studies of nucleotide-free 15N-labeled transducin α bound as a complex with Gβγ to detergent-solubilized, light-activated rhodopsin showed severe broadening of amide resonances, suggestive of structure that is dynamic in the millisecond-microsecond time scale.
source: earlier NMR studies of nucleotide-free 15N-labeled transducin α bound as a complex with Gβγ to detergent-solubilized, light-activated rhodopsin showed severe broadening of amide resonances, suggestive of structure that is dynamic in the millisecond-microsecond time scale (Abdulaev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abdulaev et al., 2006.

claim: Crystal structures may not exhibit the range of dynamic motion that is accessible to the Gαi1:GPCR complex in a lipid environment.
source: Crystal structures may not exhibit the range of dynamic motion that is accessible to the Gαi1:GPCR complex in a lipid environment.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of crystal structures.

claim: Ric-8A activation of free Gαi1•GDP destabilizes the nucleotide-binding site of Gαi1.
source: Ric-8A activation of free Gαi1•GDP, like GPCR activation of Gβγ-bound Gα•GDP, destabilizes the nucleotide-binding site of Gαi1 and induces domain separation, as demonstrated previously by DEER spectroscopy (Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by DEER spectroscopy data cited as Van Eps et al., 2015.

claim: Ric-8A activation of free Gαi1•GDP induces domain separation.
source: Ric-8A activation of free Gαi1•GDP, like GPCR activation of Gβγ-bound Gα•GDP, destabilizes the nucleotide-binding site of Gαi1 and induces domain separation, as demonstrated previously by DEER spectroscopy (Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by DEER spectroscopy data cited as Van Eps et al., 2015.

claim: The extent of structural perturbation induced in Gαi1 by Ric-8A is at least comparable to, and possibly more extensive than those resulting from the action of the β2AR on the Gαs.
source: However, the HDX data suggest that the extent of structural perturbation induced in Gαi1 by Ric-8A is at least comparable to, and possibly more extensive than those resulting from the action of the β2AR on the Gαs, as revealed by HDX studies of the β2AR:Gs complex (Chung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison based on HDX-MS data from this study and cited studies.

claim: Heteronuclear 1H-15N HSQC NMR spectra of nucleotide-free transducin α show it to be only slightly more dynamic than its GDP-bound counterpart.
source: Heteronuclear 1H-15N HSQC NMR spectra of both nucleotide-free transducin α (Gαt) (Abdulaev et al., 2006) and Gαi1 (Goricanec et al., 2016) show these α subunits to be only slightly more dynamic than their GDP-bound counterparts, the former bound to Gβγ, as assessed by the broadening of amide resonances.
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: Heteronuclear 1H-15N HSQC NMR spectra of nucleotide-free Gαi1 show it to be only slightly more dynamic than its GDP-bound counterpart.
source: Heteronuclear 1H-15N HSQC NMR spectra of both nucleotide-free transducin α (Gαt) (Abdulaev et al., 2006) and Gαi1 (Goricanec et al., 2016) show these α subunits to be only slightly more dynamic than their GDP-bound counterparts, the former bound to Gβγ, as assessed by the broadening of amide resonances.
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: NMR spectra of rhodopsin:Gαt show considerable line broadening indicative of dynamics in the millisecond-microsecond range.
source: In contrast, as described above, NMR spectra of rhodopsin:Gαt (Abdulaev et al., 2006) and Gαi1:Ric-8A (Thomas et al., 2011) show considerable line broadening indicative of dynamics in the millisecond-microsecond range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: NMR spectra of Gαi1:Ric-8A show considerable line broadening indicative of dynamics in the millisecond-microsecond range.
source: In contrast, as described above, NMR spectra of rhodopsin:Gαt (Abdulaev et al., 2006) and Gαi1:Ric-8A (Thomas et al., 2011) show considerable line broadening indicative of dynamics in the millisecond-microsecond range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: The substantial deprotection observed for many peptide segments of Gαi1 is largely due to structural changes induced by Ric-8A.
source: Thus, we would conclude that the substantial deprotection observed for many peptide segments of Gαi1 is largely due to structural changes induced by Ric-8A, which forms a stable, but dynamic complex with nucleotide-free Gαi1.

claim: Ric-8A forms a stable, but dynamic complex with nucleotide-free Gαi1.
source: Thus, we would conclude that the substantial deprotection observed for many peptide segments of Gαi1 is largely due to structural changes induced by Ric-8A, which forms a stable, but dynamic complex with nucleotide-free Gαi1.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS and NMR data.

claim: Switch II binds the GTP γ-phosphate and the Mg2+ cofactor in the activated state of Gα.
source: These two switches bind the GTP γ-phosphate and the Mg2+ cofactor in the activated state of Gα.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Gα proteins.

claim: Involvement of Switch I and Switch II in Ric-8A binding is supported by biochemical and spectroscopic evidence.
source: Involvement of these regions in Ric-8A binding is supported by the biochemical and spectroscopic evidence cited above (Thomas et al., 2011; Nagai et al., 2010; Van Eps et al., 2015).

claim: Putative contacts with Switch II explain the very weak affinity of Ric-8A for Gα•GTP.
source: Putative contacts with Switch II explain the very weak affinity of Ric-8A for Gα•GTP (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations and cited experimental observations.

claim: Switch II is well ordered in crystal structures of activated Gα proteins, stabilized by backbone amide hydrogen bonds to the GTP γ-phosphate.
source: Stabilized by backbone amide hydrogen bonds to the GTP γ-phosphate (Sprang et al., 2007), Switch II is well ordered in crystal structures of activated Gα proteins.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Binding to Ric-8A would likely require the disruption of the energetically favorable interaction between Switch II and the GTP γ-phosphate.
source: Binding to Ric-8A would likely require the disruption of this energetically favorable interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: Gβγ binds weakly to Gα•GTP for the same reason that Ric-8A does.
source: For the same reason, Gβγ, which forms an extensive interface with Switch II, also binds weakly to Gα•GTP (Higashijima et al., 1987b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higashijima et al., 1987b.

claim: Switch II is disordered in crystal structures of Gαi1•GDP.
source: In contrast, Switch II is disordered in crystal structures of Gαi1•GDP (Mixon et al., 1995) and in solution (Van Eps et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Binding of Ric-8A or Gβγ to Gαi1•GDP is facilitated because Switch II is not otherwise engaged in strong interactions.
source: Hence, binding of Ric-8A or Gβγ to Gαi1•GDP is facilitated because Switch II is not otherwise engaged in strong interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: Ric-8A and Gβγ bind competitively to Gα•GDP, sharing a common Switch II binding site.
source: Sharing a common Switch II binding site, Ric-8A and Gβγ bind competitively to Gα•GDP (Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tall et al., 2003.

claim: Ric-8A and Gβγ likely recognize different conformations of Switch II.
source: However, it is likely that they also recognize different conformations of Switch II, since Ric-8A has GEF activity, while Gβγ inhibits GDP release.
evidence: This is an inference based on their different functional effects.

claim: Ric-8A forms a large interaction surface with Gαi1.
source: In aggregate, the HDX data presented here permit the inference that Ric-8A forms a large interaction surface with Gαi1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: Interaction with Ric-8A results in protection of the Gα N-terminus, parts of the α3 and α4 helices and β6 of the Ras domain, regions within the helical domain and its interface with the Ras domain.
source: Clasping the C-terminus of Gα, and buttressed by Switch II, interaction with Ric-8A results in protection of the Gα N-terminus, parts of the α3 and α4 helices and β6 of the Ras domain, regions within the helical domain and its interface with the Ras domain (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: An extensive Ric-8A:Gαi1 interface confers stability to the dynamic and structurally heterogeneous nucleotide-free Gα.
source: We suggest that an extensive Ric-8A:Gαi1 interface confers stability to the dynamic and structurally heterogeneous nucleotide-free Gα.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The mechanism of Ric-8A as a GEF is consistent with its role as a Gα chaperone.
source: In this respect the mechanism of Ric-8A as a GEF is consistent also with its role as a Gα chaperone (Chan et al., 2013), in which a partially unstructured state of the Gα substrate is an intermediate in an enzyme-mediated catalytic event.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the GEF and chaperone functions, supported by citation.

claim: The efficiency of Ric-8A-catalyzed GEF activity is limited by the rate at which Gα is able to make the transition to a partly unfolded state during GDP release and is restored to a fully folded state upon GTP binding.
source: Thus, the efficiency of Ric-8A-catalyzed GEF activity is limited by the rate at which Gα is able to make the transition to a partly unfolded state during GDP release and is restored to a fully folded state upon GTP binding.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the data and discussion.

claim: In comparison to GPCRs, Ric-8A is a relatively inefficient GEF.
source: It is therefore not surprising that, in comparison to GPCRs, Ric-8A is a relatively inefficient GEF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic considerations discussed.
